content: 1. A study published in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 2010 examined the effects of a depression prevention program for high-risk adolescents, with follow-up assessments conducted at one and two years post-intervention. 2. Stice et al. (2011) investigated the relationship between depression and perceived social support in adolescents, using data from a randomized trial aimed at preventing adolescent depression. The findings were published in Behaviour Research and Therapy. 3. Takagaki et al. (2016) conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of behavioral activation therapy for late adolescents with subthreshold depression. The results were published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. 4. Takagaki et al. (2018) explored the long-term effects of a five-week behavioral activation program for late adolescents with subthreshold depression. This exploratory randomized controlled trial was published in Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 5. Topper et al. (2017) assessed the prevention of anxiety disorders and depression in adolescents and young adults by targeting excessive worry and rumination. The randomized controlled trial results were published in Behaviour Research and Therapy. 6. Wijnhoven et al. (2014) tested the effectiveness of a depression prevention program called Op Volle Kracht among adolescent girls with elevated depressive symptoms. The findings were published in the Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. 7. Woods and Jose (2011) evaluated the effectiveness of a school-based early intervention program for Māori and Pacific adolescents. The study was published in the Journal of Pacific Rim Psychology. 8. Wright et al. (2017) conducted a UK-based randomized controlled trial to assess the feasibility and four-month outcomes of computerized cognitive-behavioral therapy for depression in adolescents. The results were published in BMJ Open. 9. Young, Mufson, and Davies (2006) examined the efficacy of interpersonal psychotherapy-adolescent skills training (IPT-AST) as a preventive intervention for depression. The study was published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 10. Young, Gallop, and Mufson (2009) investigated the moderating effects of mother-child conflict on depression outcomes in a preventive intervention for adolescent depression. The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology. 11. Young, Mufson, and Gallop (2010) conducted a randomized trial comparing interpersonal psychotherapy-adolescent skills training (IPT-AST) to group counseling for preventing depression. The study was published in Depression and Anxiety. 12. Young et al. (2012) explored the anxiety outcomes and the impact of comorbidity in adolescents undergoing interpersonal psychotherapy-adolescent skills training (IPT-AST). The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology. 13. Young et al. (2016) compared IPT-AST to group counseling in a school-based randomized trial, focusing on long-term effects. The study was published in Prevention Science. 14. Young et al. (2018) reported on the long-term outcomes of a school-based trial comparing IPT-AST to group counseling. The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology. 15. Zandkarimi et al. (2018) conducted a randomized experiment to evaluate the effects of nonviolence communication on reducing stress, anxiety, and depression in young Iranian women. The study was published in the Child & Adolescent Social Work Journal. 16. Abdulmalik et al. (2016) examined the effects of problem-solving interventions on aggressive behaviors among primary school pupils in Ibadan, Nigeria. The findings were published in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health. 17. Asscher et al. (2013) conducted a randomized controlled trial in the Netherlands to evaluate the effectiveness of multisystemic therapy for juvenile delinquents, focusing on post-treatment changes and moderator effects. The study was published in the Journal of Experimental Criminology. 18. Asscher et al. (2014) investigated the sustainability of multisystemic therapy effects on delinquency and recidivism among juvenile delinquents in the Netherlands. The findings were published in the Journal of Experimental Criminology. 19. Avci and Kelleci (2016) evaluated the effects of an anger coping program based on cognitive-behavioral techniques on adolescents' anger, aggression, and psychological symptoms. The study was published in the International Journal of Nursing Practice. 20. Berry et al. (2009) conducted an evaluation of the Youth at Risk’s Coaching for Communities program. The findings were published in the Howard Journal of Criminal Justice. 21. Borowsky et al. (2004) assessed the effects of a primary care-based intervention on violent behavior and injury in children. The study was published in Pediatrics. 22. Currie and Startup (2012) conducted two controlled trials of percussion group psychotherapy for adolescent reactive aggression. The findings were published in the Journal of Adolescence. 23. De Vries et al. (2015) reviewed effective components of prevention programs for youth at risk of persistent juvenile delinquency, providing recommendations for clinical practice. The study was published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 24. Down et al. (2011) conducted a mixed-methods study on the efficacy and treatment preferences of anger management groups for adolescents. The findings were published in Clinical Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 25. Jalling et al. (2016) evaluated parent programs aimed at reducing adolescents' antisocial behavior and substance use through a randomized controlled trial. The study was published in the Journal of Child and Family Studies. 26. Kannappan and Bai (2008) assessed the efficacy of yoga, cognitive, and human relationship training for correcting maladjustment behavior in deviant schoolboys. The study was published in the Journal of the Indian Academy of Applied Psychology. 27. Leijten et al. (2012) evaluated the effectiveness of a parent training program during (pre)adolescence through a randomized controlled trial. The findings were published in the Journal of Adolescence. 28. Project MVP (2014) targeted high-risk, socially influential middle school students to reduce aggression, comparing universal and selective preventive intervention effects. The study was published in the Journal of Research on Adolescence. 29. Obsuth et al. (2017) reported on the London Education and Inclusion Project (LEIP), a cluster-randomized controlled trial aimed at reducing school exclusion and antisocial behavior. The findings were published in the Journal of Youth and Adolescence. 30. Perrino et al. (2016) conducted a randomized controlled trial to reduce the risk of internalizing symptoms among high-risk Hispanic youth through a family intervention. The study was published in Family Process. 31. Ranney et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of a brief emergency department-based alcohol and violence intervention on depressive symptoms. The findings were published in General Hospital Psychiatry. 32. Scheckner and Rollin (2003) described an elementary school violence prevention program. The study was published in the Journal of School Violence. 33. Shechtman (2000) conducted an outcome study on an innovative intervention for treating child and adolescent aggression. The findings were published in Psychology in the Schools. 34. Shechtman (2006) explored the contribution of bibliotherapy to counseling aggressive boys. The study was published in Psychotherapy Research. 35. Shechtman and Ifargan (2009) compared school-based integrated and segregated interventions to reduce aggression. The findings were published in Aggressive Behavior. 36. Simonsen et al. (2011) compared a behavioral check-in/check-out (CICO) intervention to standard practice in an urban middle school setting using an experimental group design. The study was published in the Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions. 37. Teeter et al. (2000) examined therapeutic interventions aimed at increasing social competence in teens with impulse control deficits. The findings were published in the Journal of Psychotherapy in Independent Practice.
